text: It's 1975 and you run Kodak, the biggest name in photography. You sell the film, the chemicals and the paper. Every holiday snap in America makes you money.

In December, a 25-year-old engineer named Steve Sasson wheels an 8-pound box into your office. It takes a 100 by 100 pixel, black-and-white picture in 23 seconds and saves it to a cassette tape. You need a TV to see it. There is no film anywhere.
It's slow, ugly and blurry. But if it ever gets good, nobody will need your film.
What do you do with the digital camera?
The film division is nervous. Whatever you pick, they'll be watching.

The film division cheers. Kodak patents the camera and keeps researching quietly, but nobody is asked to turn it into a product. Sasson later recalled executives asking why anyone would want to take pictures this way.

Protecting your best business feels safe. But a new technology that looks worse at first can still replace you, and every year you wait, someone else learns it first. What would have worked: Give digital to a small, separate team that's allowed to compete with film, and fund it from film profits.
You give Sasson twenty engineers, a separate building and one rule: don't ask the film division for permission. Film keeps paying the bills while the team learns sensors, storage and screens.
You kept the cash machine running while buying time to learn the next one. A separate team can't be strangled by the business it's meant to replace.
You rush a camera into stores. It's bulky, slow and needs a television to view anything. Almost nobody buys it, and the loss shows up in your next annual report.

Right idea, wrong year. In 1975 there were no home computers and no screens worth viewing photos on. Being first is useless if customers can't use what you sell. What would have worked: Keep developing it in a separate team, and launch when screens and storage are ready.

August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a small magnetic disk instead of film. The idea you locked away is now on the front pages, with Sony's name on it. You can still fix this.

August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a magnetic disk instead of film. Retailers panic. Your digital team isn't surprised; they've been building something similar for six years.
August 1981. Sony announces the Mavica, an electronic camera that records pictures on a magnetic disk instead of film. Your early camera flopped, but the world just caught up with the idea.
The board is uneasy about your last call. A big retailer asks what Sony's camera means for film. Investors want an answer this week.
A big retailer asks what Sony's camera means for film. Investors want an answer this week.
How do you respond to Sony?
Careful. One more bad call and the board starts asking questions about you.
Film still makes most of our money. But this time the world is watching.
The stock holds steady and the camera counters keep selling film. Inside Kodak, the message is clear: digital is not a career move. Your best engineers start taking calls from Japan.

Early versions of a disruptive product are always worse. Comparing today's quality hides the real question: how fast is it improving? What would have worked: Accept that digital is coming and start shifting money and people toward it while film is still strong.

Your market-intelligence chief, Vince Barabba, reports back: digital could replace film, but Kodak has roughly ten years to prepare. The company decides on a slow shift that keeps film profits as high as possible for as long as possible.

The study was right about the threat. The mistake was treating 'ten years' as permission to wait. A deadline is only useful if you start moving before it. What would have worked: Use the ten-year window to move money and talent into digital now, not in year nine.
You pull the 1975 prototype out of the cupboard and put its inventor in charge. It's six years late, but Kodak still has the money, the patents and the brand to catch up.
You announce that a growing share of film profits will fund digital imaging every year. Wall Street grumbles about lower margins. Your engineers stop job hunting.
You used the cash from the old business to pay for the new one while you still could. That's the move most incumbents make too late.
It's 2001. Your digital cameras are among the best sellers in America, and people are starting to put their photos online. Kodak has just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
It's 2001. Digital cameras are finally taking off and Kodak is selling them, but film is still where the money is. You've just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures.
It's 2001. Digital cameras are taking off and Kodak is late. Film sales have peaked. You've just bought Ofoto, a website where people upload pictures. This may be your best chance to catch up.
Millions of people will soon put their photos online. But Kodak still earns its money from prints, paper and chemicals.
What is Ofoto for?
This is your last warning from the board. Get this one wrong and they'll find a new CEO.
Every photo that stays on a screen is a print we never sell. But maybe that's the point.
Renamed Kodak Gallery, the site grows to over 60 million users. But free accounts must keep buying prints or risk losing their photos. People want to share pictures with friends, not pay for paper.

You built the website around your old revenue instead of what customers wanted to do. The customer's job had changed from printing memories to sharing them. What would have worked: Make it a free place to share photos with friends, and earn from the audience instead of paper.

Uploads are free, albums are easy to share, and friends comment on each other's photos. Within a few years, Kodak owns the place where families keep their pictures, just as phones start getting cameras.
You followed the customer's new habit, sharing, even though it hurt print sales. Owning the audience is worth more than owning the paper.
Kodak cameras fly off the shelves and the brand looks modern again. But every competitor is selling cameras too, and prices fall every year.

Cameras were a real business, but a crowded one with thin margins. You gave up the part of digital that customers come back to every day. What would have worked: Keep the website and make it about sharing. That's where people would spend their time.
It's 2006. Film sales are collapsing across the industry, but your digital businesses are growing fast enough to carry the company. You have a strong hand. Don't waste it.
It's 2006. Film sales are collapsing. Your digital business is real but not yet big enough to replace what film used to earn. This is your last big decision.
It's 2006. Film sales are collapsing and your factories are closing one by one. Phones are starting to have cameras. This is your last chance to save the company.
You have patents, chemistry expertise, factories and a famous name. Film won't come back.
Where do you bet the company's future?
Whatever we pick, we can only afford to do it properly once.
You win shelf space, then lose money on every price cut. Within a few years, the phone in everyone's pocket takes good enough pictures, and the standalone camera market starts to shrink.

You chose a market where prices only go down and a bigger threat, the phone, was already arriving. What would have worked: Use what Kodak is best at, chemistry and materials, to enter new growing markets.
In February 2007 Kodak launched EasyShare all-in-one printers, promising ink at a fraction of rivals' prices. Customers liked the price, but fewer and fewer of them were printing photos at all.

Cheaper ink was a smart pitch for a shrinking habit. You bet on people printing photos at home just as they started keeping them on screens. What would have worked: Use Kodak's chemistry and materials know-how to enter new growing markets, as Fujifilm did.

You cut costs hard in film, then point your chemists at medical imaging, specialty films and materials. It's painful and slow, but new businesses start replacing what film used to earn. Fujifilm made a similar move and is still thriving.
You asked what Kodak was really good at, chemistry and materials, instead of what it used to sell. Skills travel to new markets; products don't.
By 2012, Kodak is a digital imaging and materials company. Film is a small, profitable corner of the business. Business schools teach your story as the incumbent that disrupted itself.
Kodak shrinks a lot, but it never goes bankrupt. You fixed enough, late enough, to keep the lights on. With a few earlier calls, it could have led the digital age.

On January 19, 2012, Kodak files for bankruptcy. That April, Facebook buys Instagram, a photo-sharing app with 13 employees, for one billion dollars. The company that invented the digital camera lost the digital age.
Three bad calls. The board loses faith and replaces you. Your successor inherits a company that's falling behind, and the clock is still ticking.
